title: what namaste actually says
hook: the word at the end of yoga class is how a lot of the world says hello

segments.voice: Yesterday: memento mori, and while you can, be good. Today, the word at the end of yoga class.

Class ends. Everyone sits up, palms together, and the teacher says namaste. Then there's the mug that says namaste in bed. In much of India and Nepal, it isn't a yoga word at all. It's how you greet your aunt, your neighbor, a guest at the door. And what it says is plainer, and kinder, than most people think. First, a guess.
screen: `PALMS TOGETHER. NAMASTE.` → `NOT A YOGA WORD.` → `HOW YOU GREET YOUR AUNT.`

segments.voice: Namaste is Sanskrit, in two pieces. Namas, a bow. Te, to you. A bow to you. People say it to elders, guests and strangers, usually with the palms pressed together at the chest and a small dip of the head. Sometimes the gesture says it with no word at all. You may have heard it means the light in me honors the light in you. That's a modern reading, not a translation. It draws on a real idea some Hindu teachers find in the bow: that something sacred lives in every person, so you're bowing to that, not to someone's job or mood. So is it okay to say it in a yoga class? Hindus don't all feel the same way about that, and it's worth knowing they differ. What tends to sting is the word as a punchline: on a beer can, or as a joke for leave me alone. What tends to land is the plain thing it is: a greeting, meant. The difference isn't who's saying it. It's whether the bow is real.
screen: `NAMAS — A BOW.` · `TE — TO YOU.` · `THE LIGHT LINE IS A READING.` · `A GREETING, MEANT.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Bring your palms together at your chest, if you'd like. On the first breath, feel your hands meet. On the second, bring to mind someone you'll see today. On the third, a small bow of the head, toward them, wherever they are.
Namaste. Namas, a bow; te, to you. A hello with respect inside it. Fourth word.
Your line: mean the bow. Said that way, it's what it has always been in India and Nepal: a real greeting. Day four.

howItsDone: In India and Nepal, people greet elders, guests and strangers with namaste or namaskar, palms pressed together at the chest and the head slightly bowed; many Hindus make the same gesture before images of the gods.

original.note: Sanskrit: namas, a bow, plus te, to you. Namaskar is the same bow, as a noun.

trapdoor: what you thought: a yoga sign-off.
what it means: a bow to you, an everyday greeting with the palms together.
what a scholar hears: Sanskrit namas (a bow, homage) + te (to you); namaskar is namas + kara, making: the act of bowing.

story.title: the man on the narrow path
story.text: A famous teacher is walking down to the river to bathe when a man with four dogs blocks the narrow path. By the rules of the day the man is an outcaste, and he's told to move aside. He answers with a question: what should move, this body made of food, or the self inside it, which is the same as yours? The teacher stops, and bows to him.
story.source: the legend behind the Manisha Panchakam, a hymn traditionally credited to Adi Shankara (Varanasi); told in several versions

wrong.myth: namaste literally means the light in me honors the light in you.
wrong.truth: literally it's namas, a bow, and te, to you. the light line is a reading of the bow.

notes: New lesson (2026-10-06) from the research's proposed day 4 (Top 20 #5). Karma, which the research pairs with namaste, has its own day (7).
Consistent with the Hindu path's day 4: word for word 'I bow to you'; the 'light' line is a reading, not a translation (Chandogya 3.13.7 named in sources only).

Sensitive: whether non-Hindus using namaste in yoga is respectful. The script says Hindus differ, names the punchline uses that tend to sting, and does not rule for or against. A Hindu Keeper should check the tone.

Sensitive: the story involves caste ('by the rules of the day the man is an outcaste'). The legend's point is against that rule; the telling avoids the word chandala. In some versions Shankara himself, not his students, tells the man to move; the script uses the passive. Confirm.
Namaste in Nepal and India: also used by many non-Hindus in those countries, though Sikhs, Muslims and others often have their own greetings; the script says 'in much of India and Nepal'. Confirm.
